First Nations leaders and some premiers are gathering in Ottawa on Monday, Oct. 26, for a closed-door meeting with Prime Minister Mark Carney, the first dedicated First Nations–first ministers gathering since 2005. Ahead of the talks, leaders held ceremony in Ottawa on Sunday and said they want an ongoing role in resource-development decisions as federal and provincial governments move to accelerate major-project approvals. Assembly of First Nations (AFN) National Chief Cindy Woodhouse Nepinak has called for the meeting to begin an ongoing relationship, while some chiefs question whether the restricted format will give them meaningful input. Alberta Premier Danielle Smith and Quebec Premier Paul St-Pierre Plamondon will not attend. The federal government says it plans to announce new community supports on Monday.

items.title: [cbc.ca] Carney and Ford commit $8.7 billion to tariff-hit Ontario industries
items.content_html:
🪶 ✏️

Prime Minister Mark Carney and Ontario Premier Doug Ford announced an $8.7-billion federal-provincial package on Oct. 21 for Ontario’s steel and auto industries and roads to the mineral-rich Ring of Fire region. The plan allocates about $5.2 billion to steel over five years, $2.5 billion to autos over two years and up to $1 billion in federal funding for roads over three years, matching Ontario’s contribution. The governments say the investments will help mills modernize, support auto production and reduce reliance on U.S. markets as tariffs disrupt trade. The package also includes stronger enforcement against steel dumping, a joint steel task force and a coordinated process for mine permits. A working group will engage First Nations on economic development and conservation, including possible Indigenous protected areas.

items.title: [bankier.pl] Alberta rejects separation vote as First Nations legal challenge continues
items.content_html:
🪶 ✏️

Alberta voters rejected starting the legal process for a binding separation referendum, with about 75% choosing to remain in Canada and 25% backing the process in the Oct. 19 vote, according to the complete but unofficial count. Elections Alberta expects to release official results on Oct. 29. Voters supported proposals on immigration and citizenship rules but rejected all four proposed constitutional changes. Premier Danielle Smith has said she will pursue the measures that passed and work with Prime Minister Mark Carney on immigration. Separately, the Alberta government is continuing its appeal of a ruling that quashed a citizen-led separation petition. First Nations chiefs and Alberta’s opposition are urging it to withdraw the appeal; the government says the court decision contained errors of law.

Separately, the Alberta government is continuing its appeal of a ruling that quashed a citizen-led separation petition. First Nations chiefs and Alberta’s opposition are urging it to withdraw the appeal; the government says the court decision contained errors of law (cbc.ca). Rural divide: Only two ridings had majority support for moving toward a separation vote: Rimbey-Rocky Mountain House-Sundre, at 51.1%, and Central Peace-Notley, at 50.4%. Support was 15% in Edmonton and 18% in Calgary (edmontonjournal.com, theglobeandmail.com). Constitutional proposals: The four rejected proposals covered electing judges, abolishing the Senate, opting out of some federal programs while keeping funding, and allowing provincial laws to override conflicting federal laws. Each would require support from other provinces (nationalobserver.com). Petition threshold: The separatist group Stay Free Alberta gathered more than 300,000 signatures, nearly twice the legal threshold (calgaryherald.com). Turnout: Nearly 2.1 million people voted, about 64% of eligible voters, in the province’s largest electoral event (catholicregister.org, theglobeandmail.com, bankier.pl).

items.title: [news.un.org] UN urges steep fossil-fuel cuts as 1.5°C overshoot becomes unavoidable
items.content_html:
🪶 ✏️

The United Nations Environment Programme’s (UNEP) 2026 Emissions Gap Report says governments must now limit the scale and duration of global warming beyond 1.5°C, rather than try to prevent that threshold from being crossed. Its lowest-overshoot pathway would cap warming at 1.7°C to 1.8°C around mid-century, with about a 50% chance of returning to 1.5°C by 2100. Following that pathway requires greenhouse-gas emissions to fall 18% by 2030, 45% by 2035 and 69% by 2040, compared with 2025. The report says existing national climate pledges would cut emissions by only 5% to 8% by 2030 and 11% to 15% by 2035. If current policies continue, warming could reach 2.8°C this century; full delivery of pledges would still leave it at about 2.6°C. The pathway also calls for sharply reducing coal-fired electricity generation and scaling up carbon removal. The report warns that the required reductions are far beyond current plans. Governments are due to discuss climate action at the COP31 summit, scheduled to open in Antalya on Nov. 9.

Russian President Vladimir Putin agreed in principle to resume U.S.-mediated talks with Ukraine after Nov. 10, following a nearly three-hour meeting on Oct. 21 with U.S. special envoy Steve Witkoff in St. Petersburg. Kremlin foreign-policy adviser Yuri Ushakov said the technical-level negotiations could take place in Abu Dhabi and focus on a postwar security framework for Russia and Ukraine. Earlier rounds yielded little progress beyond prisoner exchanges. Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said Kyiv supports resuming the talks as soon as possible, preferably by early November, and proposed freezing the current front line as a first step toward a ceasefire. He also called for Ukraine to be included in decisions about its future and said Ukraine’s parliament must approve any peace settlement. Witkoff brought Putin proposals discussed a day earlier with Zelenskyy and European officials in Oslo, including security guarantees and postwar arrangements. Ushakov said the proposals contained little useful material. Moscow continues to seek terms Kyiv rejects, including Russian control of all of Donetsk and a bar on Ukrainian NATO membership. A technical-level meeting is the next step, but no firm date or venue has been announced. The Kremlin said talks could begin after Nov. 10.

A study published in Science says the Barnes Ice Cap on Canada’s Baffin Island, the last remnant of the Laurentide Ice Sheet, began expanding about 2,000 years ago. Researchers identify that growth as the start of a new glacial period. The ice began retreating around 1960 as summer warming caused it to lose more ice than it gained. The team reconstructed the ice cap’s history using vegetation preserved beneath the ice and dates from exposed rocks. The researchers define the start of a glacial period as the resumption of ice-sheet growth, differing from models that place the next glaciation thousands or tens of thousands of years in the future. Models cited by the researchers project that the Barnes Ice Cap could disappear within the next few centuries. The researchers say rising atmospheric carbon dioxide makes a return to glacial conditions extremely unlikely.

The ice began retreating around 1960 as summer warming caused it to lose more ice than it gained (columbia.edu, science.org, wired.com). The team reconstructed the ice cap’s history using vegetation preserved beneath the ice and dates from exposed rocks. The researchers define the start of a glacial period as the resumption of ice-sheet growth, differing from models that place the next glaciation thousands or tens of thousands of years in the future (phys.org, reddit.com). Models cited by the researchers project that the Barnes Ice Cap could disappear within the next few centuries. The researchers say rising atmospheric carbon dioxide makes a return to glacial conditions extremely unlikely (columbia.edu, tagesspiegel.de). Ice margin record: The edge has receded an average of 4 meters a year since the 1980s (wired.com). Regional evidence: Researchers combined analyses of the Barnes Ice Cap with evidence from smaller, recently melted ice caps to reconstruct the region’s climate history (columbia.edu). Ice cap sensitivity: The Barnes Ice Cap rests on bedrock about 500 meters above sea level. The share of its surface above the local snowline fell from about 35% in 1960–1980 to 3% in 2000–2012, and it has had no accumulation area since 2010 (reddit.com).

Perspective: Shaun Marcott, University of Wisconsin-Madison geoscientist: Marcott warned that the absence of future glacial cycles could affect biological and physical Earth systems that evolved alongside them, and urged consideration of what an ice-free world could mean (Tagesspiegel)

items.title: [Fast Company] The U.S. Treasury wants expanded restrictions on high-tech investments to these ‘countries of concern’
items.content_html:
🪶 ✏️

The U.S. Treasury Department proposed a rule Thursday to crack down on American high-tech investments such as supercomputing and artificial intelligence in China, Russia, North Korea and other “countries of concern.”

The U.S. government has been working for years to deny China and other adversaries investments that could help them boost their military power.

That program began in 2023 when then-President Joe Biden signed an executive order putting restrictions on outbound U.S. investments in sectors such as semiconductors, quantum computing and artificial intelligence going into China. Treasury later established the Outbound Investment Security Program.

In December 2025, Congress passed a law that codified and expanded the program to target more technologies and more foreign countries, including Cuba, Iran, North Korea and Russia.

The inclusion of Russia in the proposed rule has come days after President Donald Trump waived sanctions on Russia following a diesel deal with President Vladimir Putin.

The rule announced Thursday would expand the restrictions to cover investments in hypersonic systems capable of traveling at five times the speed of sound, supercomputing, biotechnology and artificial intelligence, though Treasury used Trump’s favored term for AI, “superintelligence” or SI.

The proposed rule “sends an important signal to markets that Washington is tracking where U.S. capital is flowing and what capabilities it is helping build,” said Craig Singleton, a senior fellow at the think tank Foundation for Defense of Democracies.

The screening of outbound investments “recognizes that capital can accelerate military-relevant capabilities just as surely as technology transfer can,” Singleton said.

Jason Chipman, a former Justice Department lawyer who specializes in cybersecurity, investment rules and export controls as a partner at the law firm WilmerHale, said the new rule “will require more substantial compliance programs to manage risk.”

Treasury’s rule to implement the 2025 law — the Comprehensive Outbound Investment National Security Act — would only apply to investments that exceed $50,000 and would exclude many financial investments, including stock purchases.

Treasury will hear public comments on the proposal before issuing a final rule.

“It’s just the first step in a fairly long process to get to changes which presumably will be more enforcement-minded, to put more teeth behind the outbound investment program,” said former U.S. trade official Ryan Majerus, now a partner at King & Spalding law firm.

In Beijing, the Chinese Foreign Ministry said the U.S. should abide by the principles of a market economy and stop interfering in normal economic and trade cooperation between businesses.

Asked about Washington’s proposal to add biotechnology to the list, ministry spokesperson Mao Ning said that “Overstretching the concept of national security, taking discriminatory measures against specific countries, and artificially restricting trade, economic and investment activities serve no one’s interests.”

She added that China will closely monitor relevant developments and take necessary measures to safeguard its interests.

Since Trump’s first term, the United States and China — the world’s two biggest economies — have been locked in an economic and tech rivalry. They’ve restricted the export of sensitive technology and critical products — such as China’s rare earth minerals and America’s advanced computer chips — to each other and slapped tariffs on each other’s products. Trump and Chinese President Xi Jinping agreed last year to ease tensions while they engaged in talks, a temporary truce they last month extended into January.

But the sparring continues. In July, the Treasury Department issued a $200,000 fine against a U.S.-based company for failing to report to the department a $92,500 investment in a Chinese artificial intelligence and robotics company by one of its subsidiaries.

—Paul Wiseman and Didi Tang, Associated Press

items.title: [thehackernews.com] Attackers compromise AI gateway LiteLLM 1.107.0 to steal credentials
items.content_html:
🪶 ✏️

Attackers released a malicious version of LiteLLM, an open-source gateway for connecting to AI models, distributing version 1.107.0 through the Python Package Index (PyPI) and Docker images on Oct. 21. The package installed a credential stealer and a backdoor that could collect cloud and AI service keys, private keys, browser data and other secrets. The code could run whenever Python started, even in programs that did not use LiteLLM. LiteLLM said attackers used three engineers’ GitHub credentials to alter and approve the release, but it has not identified how they obtained those credentials. PyPI removed the package, and affected Docker image tags were removed or replaced. The company advised users to rebuild from a clean environment, rotate exposed credentials and use version 1.106.2 while the investigation continues.

The package installed a credential stealer and a backdoor that could collect cloud and AI service keys, private keys, browser data and other secrets. The code could run whenever Python started, even in programs that did not use LiteLLM (thehackernews.com, safedep.io, theregister.com). Build integrity: SafeDep, which analyzed the compromised package, found that the public v1.107.0 GitHub tag did not contain the payload. Image tags: The compromised Docker images included the floating tags latest, main-latest and main-stable, so users could pull them without explicitly requesting version 1.107.0 (reddit.com, safedep.io, ithome.com.tw). Data exposure: The stealer could extract stored provider keys from LiteLLM proxy database tables when a database connection was available, in addition to credentials held elsewhere on the host (safedep.io, reddit.com). Scale and warning: LiteLLM receives about 23 million weekly downloads. Security researchers urged teams to investigate any host or continuous integration (CI) runner where Python ran after installation (theregister.com).
